name: R (ClientEarth) v Secretary of State for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs
date: 1 May 2013 (UKSC, reference to the CJEU); 19 November 2014 (CJEU, C-404/13); 29 April 2015 (UKSC); 2 November 2016 and 21 February 2018 (High Court)

jurisdiction.court: Supreme Court (2013, 2015); Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) – Second Chamber (2014, preliminary ruling); High Court (2016, 2018)

description: Trilogy of court actions brought by the NGO ClientEarth against the British government (DEFRA) for failure to adopt air quality plans suitable for returning within the EU limits for NO2 (Directive 2008/50/EC) “in the shortest possible time” in several areas of the United Kingdom, in particular London.
outcome: Three consecutive victories for ClientEarth. On a reference from the UK Supreme Court ([2013] UKSC 25), the CJEU (Second Chamber, 19 November 2014, C-404/13) held that a Member State which cannot meet the NO2 limit values by the 2010 deadline must apply for a postponement and establish an air quality plan; that, where it has not done so, the adoption of a plan complying with Article 23 does not in itself mean that it has met its obligations under Article 13; and that the national court must take any necessary measure, such as an order, so that the authority establishes the plan required by the Directive. Applying that ruling, the UK Supreme Court (April 2015) ordered the government to produce new air quality plans; in 2016 and 2018 the High Court declared the subsequent plans unlawful as well, holding them inadequate under Article 23 of the Directive and the Air Quality Standards Regulations 2010, and requiring their revision within tight time limits.
